cards.title: HealthCare.gov, opening day
cards.body: The US federal insurance marketplace, run by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Outages began within two hours of launch. The site saw 250,000 concurrent users; the U.S. CTO put that at five times the number of simultaneous users anticipated. Only six consumers submitted an application and selected a plan that first day.
cards.prompt: On HealthCare.gov's opening day, how many concurrent users arrived compared with the number planned for, and how many people actually finished enrolling?
cards.answer: About 250,000 concurrent users, which the U.S. CTO put at five times the number anticipated; six people completed an application and selected a plan.

cards.title: The Terremark manager
cards.body: CMS technical officials tested the build at CGI Federal's offices, found capacity far below plan, and drove to their hosting contractor demanding double. A Terremark manager, quoted later: "We were pulling gear from all over the world, renting planes to get hardware here that was intended for other clients."
cards.prompt: Days before launch, CMS discovered its capacity estimate was wrong. What did correcting it look like physically, for the contractor who had to deliver it?
cards.answer: Doubling all purchased computing capacity in three days: Terremark pulled hardware earmarked for other clients from around the world and chartered planes to fly it in.

cards.title: OEI-06-14-00350
cards.body: "HealthCare.gov: Case Study of CMS Management of the Federal Marketplace", issued 22 February 2016. Built on interviews with 86 current and former HHS and CMS officials, staff and contractors, plus thousands of internal documents. It is the source of the 250,000-concurrent-user figure and the six-enrollment day.
cards.prompt: Which single published document reconstructs the HealthCare.gov launch failure from the inside, and what evidence base was it built on?
cards.answer: HHS Office of Inspector General report OEI-06-14-00350 (2016), built on 86 interviews with HHS, CMS and contractor staff and thousands of internal documents.

cards.title: The fix was arithmetic, done late
cards.body: CMS doubled the number of servers, added virtual machines for the Enterprise Identity Management (EIDM) and FFM systems, and swapped EIDM's virtual database for a high-capacity physical one. Availability went from 42.9 percent to just over 93 percent during November 2013; FFM response time fell from 8 seconds to under 1 second.
cards.prompt: HealthCare.gov did eventually work. What did CMS actually change, and what did availability and response time do?
cards.answer: Capacity, not cleverness: servers doubled, virtual machines added, EIDM's database moved to physical hardware. Availability 42.9% to just over 93% in November 2013; FFM response time 8 seconds to under 1 second by December 2013.
